title: Second Tail: what changed when I stopped asking coding agents to review their own work
author: parmuzin1992
selftext:
I’m making a free browser platformer about my two pet rats, Sal and Ben. Sal can double jump and Ben can dash, so getting home through the city takes both of them. It runs on desktop and phones.

I write the tickets, direct the game and play the changes myself. Claude Code and Codex agents work on the Unity C# in separate worktrees. The first version of my workflow just told agents to review their work; review was skipped on three tickets in one night. I moved that step into a git hook: a fresh reviewer sees the diff without the ticket text before the code can reach main.

The simulation runs at a fixed 1/120-second step, so I can run most logic checks outside Unity and compare recorded playthroughs by hash. For visual changes I use screenshots, then inspect the actual game myself. This week playtesters found the start too slow, so I played in the editor while an agent fixed each problem and the editor recompiled. The game now starts in play and resumes progress automatically.

AI disclosure: the code was written with Claude Code and Codex; AI-generated art is cut into parts and animated in the game. One boss uses a Blender 3D model rendered to 2D. Music includes Suno tracks and CC0 recordings.

The demo is free, with no signup: [https://para1992.itch.io/second-tail](https://para1992.itch.io/second-tail)

For anyone using agents on a game: how do you check that a change actually plays correctly rather than only passing the tests?
